query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post-deformation, low‐temperature annealing treatment that promotes the in situ formation of a fine, coherent L12 nanoprecipitate dispersion along or near the lamellar colony interfaces will simultaneously boost yield/ultimate tensile strength and arrest microcrack propagation, thereby improving room‐temperature tensile ductility relative to the conventional continuous lamellar microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) in its as-cast or cold-/cryo-rolled state having dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal (and sometimes semi‐coherent) boundaries that serve as microcrack initiation sites.
generation.intervention: A single-step, controlled low-temperature annealing treatment after deformation designed to induce fine, uniformly distributed coherent L12 precipitates within the soft FCC lamella and at the colony interfaces.
generation.conditions: The annealing should be performed at a temperature (e.g., around 580°C) and for a duration (e.g., ~24 hours) sufficient to trigger nano-precipitation without excessive coarsening, in a post-deformation (e.g., cryo or hybrid rolling) processing route.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale, coherent L12 precipitates that decorate the lamellar interfaces as well as reside within the soft FCC regions, thereby refining the microstructure and increasing the density of internal interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The coherent nanoprecipitates produce substantial back-stress hardening by pinning dislocations and inhibiting their motion, while also providing effective crack-arresting sites at the lamellar boundaries. This dual action enhances the material’s load-bearing capacity and retards microcrack coalescence, mitigating the strength–ductility trade-off.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline, the intervention should yield an alloy with a higher yield/ultimate tensile strength (e.g., with increments on the order of several hundred MPa) and improved room-temperature ductility (evidenced by a higher uniform elongation) with a finer and more damage-tolerant lamellar microstructure.
generation.baseline: The conventional eutectic HEA with continuous lamellar colonies that, while providing high strength, suffers from microcrack initiation and limited tensile ductility due to poorly tolerated internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective in eutectic HEAs with lamellar architectures (such as AlCoCrFeNi2.1 or similar compositions) where the lamella spacing and chemical inhomogeneity are within a range that allows the controlled precipitation of nano-coherent L12 particles without leading to deleterious coarsening or embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from studies on L12 precipitation (PMC6478865, PMC6478865::web::015) and on dual heterogeneous microstructures (PMC6687781::web::015) supports the potential of interface engineering to improve ductility, it remains uncertain how scaling these effects via post-deformation annealing will translate quantitatively in different processing histories of EHEAs. The exact annealing parameters (temperature/time) and their window of effectiveness need further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA samples processed identically up to a severe deformation step (e.g., cryo-rolling or hybrid rolling). Subject one set to the prescribed low-temperature annealing treatment aimed at inducing fine L12 precipitation and leave the second set as a control (no post-deformation annealing). Use high-resolution TEM/APT to characterize the nanoprecipitate size/distribution and in situ fracture testing or microcantilever bending to assess microcrack activity at colony boundaries.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves to extract yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation
Microstructural analysis (TEM, APT) quantifying precipitate size, density, and location
Fractography or in situ imaging to evaluate microcrack initiation and propagation characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed specimens do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the control, or if the intended nanoprecipitate dispersion is not achieved (or if precipitate coarsening reduces ductility), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Effect of microstructure on mechanical properties
cited_evidence.text: The advantage of such a two-phase eutectic alloy is that it consists of a more easily deformable ductile (fcc or fcc + L12) phase, and a hard, difficult to deform, B2 + bcc phase. The hard B2 + bcc phase defines the inter-lamellar spacing of the softer fcc phase. To evaluate the mechanical performance of the Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy, the CR-H and CR-H-580 conditions were tested under two different strain rates (10−3 s−1 and 2 × 103 s−1) and the corresponding stress-strain plots are shown in Fig. 6. Figure 6(a) shows the engineering (thick line) and true (thin line) stress-strain plots from quasi-static testing. The CR-H condition with fcc + B2 (with fine scale bcc precipitates) shows a yield strength (YS) of ~770 MPa, UTS ~1090 MPa with an elongation to failure (EF) of ~17% under the quasi-static deformation (10−3). The CR-H-580 condition with the fcc + L12 & B2 + bcc microstructure exhibited a YS ~1080 MPa, UTS ~1370 MPa and EF of ~15%. A precipitation strengthening of ~310 MPa is observed after the additional heat treatment with just ~2% reduction in the elongation.

Unlike microstructural heterogeneities, which have been investigated so far to achieve strength-ductility synergy in different materials,, including HEAs,,, the novel strategy developed in the present research leads to a different paradigm featured by dual structural-compositional heterogeneities. On the microstructural side, the heterogeneities are ensured by the presence of the LRs and NCRs, while on the compositional side it is featured by a number of different constituents. While the LRs consist of L12 and B2 (containing disordered nano-precipitates), the NCRs contain different ordered and disordered phases with differences in structure, composition and internal strain or defect densities. Evidently, the dual structural-compositional heterogeneities offer a large number of interfaces and boundaries separating widely different hardness domains and phases. The massive back-stress strengthening in such heterogeneous microstructural arrangements results in super-strong EHEA coupled with appreciable ductility.
